read.sections.0.heading.source: Art that does not last, memory that does
read.sections.0.heading.back: Art that does not last, memory that lasts

read.sections.0.text.source:
An artwork does not have to last for centuries to matter. Flowers, food, paper and short-lived structures can bring people together around a shared memory. In Mexico, Día de Muertos, or Day of the Dead, joins artistic making with remembering people after their death. Its meanings belong to living communities, whose practices keep changing.

UNESCO recognises the festival as practised by Mexico's Indigenous communities. It lists it as intangible heritage: knowledge and practices passed between people. UNESCO's account describes celebrations in late October and early November. This is near the end of the season when maize grows. For people who hold this belief, relatives who have died return for a short time. Families prepare favourite foods. They arrange flowers, candles and paper decorations. These actions keep up bonds between generations. They help people feel part of a community. You can study this belief without sharing it.
read.sections.0.text.back:
An artwork does not need to last for centuries to be important. Flowers, food, paper and structures that do not last long can bring people together around one shared memory. In Mexico, Día de Muertos, or Day of the Dead, combines making art with remembering people after they have passed away. Its meanings belong to communities that are living, and their practices keep changing.

UNESCO recognises this festival as it is practised by Indigenous communities in Mexico. UNESCO lists it as intangible heritage, that is, knowledge and practices passed on between people. UNESCO's account describes celebrations in late October and early November. This time is near the end of the season when maize grows. For people who hold this belief, relatives who have passed away return for a while. Families prepare their favourite foods. Families arrange flowers, candles and paper decorations. These actions keep up bonds between generations. These actions help people feel part of a community. You can learn about this belief without sharing that belief.
read.sections.0.text.note: "died" is "meninggal dunia", the gentle Malay word; "Day of the Dead" is "Hari Orang Mati", the usual Malay name for the festival. Reviewer to check the tone.

read.sections.0.simpler.source:
Art does not have to last to matter. Flowers, food and paper can bring people together to remember. In Mexico, Día de Muertos means Day of the Dead. People make art to keep the dead in mind. It belongs to living people, and it keeps changing.

UNESCO says Indigenous groups in Mexico practise it. It calls it intangible heritage. That means skills and ways that people pass on. It comes in late October and early November. That is when the maize, or corn, season ends. Some people believe that relatives who have died come back for a short time. Families cook the foods these relatives liked. They set out flowers, candles and paper. This links old and young. It helps them feel they belong. You can learn about a belief and not share it.
read.sections.0.simpler.back:

People make art to remember those who have passed away. This festival belongs to people who are still living, and this festival keeps changing.

UNESCO says Indigenous groups in Mexico practise it. UNESCO calls it intangible heritage. That means skills and ways that people pass on. This festival happens in late October and early November. At that time the maize season ends. Some people believe that relatives who have passed away come back for a while. Families cook the food those relatives liked. read.sections.1.heading.source: Histories of change, many local forms
read.sections.1.heading.back: Histories of change, many local forms

read.sections.1.text.source:
These practices have histories of change. In the sixteenth century, Europeans brought Catholic feasts to Mexico. Indigenous religious traditions became linked with them. All Saints' Day falls on 1 November, and All Souls' Day on 2 November. Religious images and older practices could take on meanings together. But not every Indigenous people, Mexican family or Catholic community celebrates in the same way. Place, family traditions and beliefs shape different forms.

For example, in the Huasteca region the festival is called Xantolo. It includes processions, or walking parades, with masked performers called Huehues. UNESCO's account says that costumes, music and characters differ from one community to the next. So a national festival name holds many local histories. A public museum display also has a different setting and audience from an ofrenda in a family home. An ofrenda is an offering. The word also means the arranged altar or display of offerings.
read.sections.1.text.back:
These practices have histories of change. In the 16th century, Europeans brought Catholic feasts to Mexico. Indigenous religious traditions became connected with them. All Saints' Day falls on 1 November, and All Souls' Day on 2 November. Religious images and older practices could take on meanings together. But not every Indigenous people, Mexican family or Catholic community celebrates in the same way. Place, family traditions and beliefs shape different forms.

For example, in the Huasteca region this festival is called Xantolo. This festival includes processions, that is, lines of people walking together, with masked performers called Huehues. UNESCO's account says that costumes, music and characters differ from one community to another. So a national festival name holds many local histories. A public museum display also has a different setting and audience from an ofrenda in a family's home. An ofrenda is an offering. The word also means the arranged altar or display of offerings.
read.sections.1.text.note: "All Saints' Day" and "All Souls' Day" are "Hari Semua Orang Kudus" and "Hari Semua Arwah"; reviewer to check the names Malaysian Catholics use. "offering" is "persembahan" (an offering to God or spirits); reviewer to confirm.

read.sections.1.simpler.source:
These ways have changed. In the 1500s, Europeans brought Catholic feast days to Mexico. Old Indigenous ways became linked with them. All Saints' Day is on 1 November, and All Souls' Day on 2 November. Old ways and Catholic images came to share meanings. But not every family or group does the same. Place, family and belief make each one its own.

In the Huasteca region, the festival is called Xantolo. People walk in a line, with masked performers called Huehues. UNESCO says the clothes, music and roles differ from group to group. So one name holds many local stories. An ofrenda is an offering. It is also the altar where offerings are set out. A museum ofrenda is for the public. It differs from one in a home.
read.sections.1.simpler.back:
These practices have changed. In the 1500s, Europeans brought Catholic feast days to Mexico. Old Indigenous ways became connected with them. All Saints' Day is on 1 November, and All Souls' Day on 2 November. Old ways and Catholic images began to share meanings. But not every family or group does it in the same way. Place, family and belief make each one different.

In the Huasteca region, this festival is called Xantolo. People walk in a line, with masked performers called Huehues. UNESCO says the costumes, music and characters differ between groups. So one name holds many local stories. An ofrenda is an offering. An ofrenda is also the altar where offerings are arranged. An ofrenda in a museum is for the public. That ofrenda is different from an ofrenda in a home.

read.sections.2.heading.source: Paper, arrangement and a printed skeleton
read.sections.2.heading.back: Paper, arrangement and a printed skeleton

read.sections.2.text.source:
An ofrenda gives memory a shape people can see. Photographs, food, flowers and other objects can show who is being remembered. They also make the space welcoming. The museum example in the photograph is in Coyoacán, in Mexico City. It has stepped levels, bright paper decoration and model skeleton figures. Its file record says it is dedicated to the Virgin of Guadalupe. This display brings Catholic images and festive making together in one public space. It cannot stand for every household altar.

Papel picado, paper with cut-out designs, needs knowledge of pattern and material. Makers cut designs into thin tissue paper and join the sheets into banners. Skilled artisans can cut several layers at once, repeating a design. The paper may not last long, but the knowledge of making it continues. Setting up a short-lived altar also takes planning, choices and work. The finished photograph shows only part of this.

Printed images have also changed how the festival looks in public. José Guadalupe Posada's Calavera Catrina shows a skeleton wearing a grand hat. A calavera is a skull, or an artistic image of a skull or skeleton. Posada's skeleton pictures used satire: humour that criticises behaviour or power. Later artists helped make his image widely known. Its later link with Día de Muertos is one chapter in a longer history. Posada did not invent the older celebration. Together, the print and the museum ofrenda show how old practices, new art and changing audiences can keep a tradition alive.
read.sections.2.text.back:
An ofrenda gives memory a shape that people can see. Photos, food, flowers and other objects can show who is being remembered. These objects also make the space feel welcoming. The museum example in the photo is in Coyoacán, in Mexico City. That ofrenda has stepped levels, bright paper decoration and models of human skeletons. Its file record says that the ofrenda is dedicated to Our Lady of Guadalupe. This display brings Catholic images and festive making together in one public space. This display cannot represent every altar in a home.

Papel picado, that is, paper with cut designs, needs knowledge of pattern and material. Makers cut designs into thin tissue paper and join the sheets into banners. Skilled craftspeople can cut several layers at once, repeating one design. The paper may not last long, but the knowledge of how to make it continues. Setting up an altar that does not last long also needs planning, choices and work. The finished photo shows only part of it.

A calavera is a skull, or an artistic image of a skull or skeleton. Posada's skeleton pictures used satire, that is, humour that criticises behaviour or power. Later artists helped make his image famous. Its later link with Día de Muertos is one chapter in a longer history. Posada did not invent that older celebration. Together, the print and the museum ofrenda show how old practices, new art and changing audiences can keep a tradition alive.

secondVisual.alt.source: A white museum room with an ofrenda built in stepped levels, each edged with bright pink cut paper. A carpet of flowers and fruit lies on the floor in front. Life-size dressed skeleton models stand on both sides.

sensitiveNotes.0.source: This lesson is about death and remembrance, and some learners may be grieving, including after losses linked to displacement. No one is asked to share about people they have lost, to describe a death, or to perform or take part in any practice. Don't ask for a bereavement example: the Write task uses only the photograph and the reading.
sensitiveNotes.0.back: This lesson is about death and remembering, and some learners may be grieving, including after losses connected with displacement. No one is asked to talk about people they have lost, to describe a death, or to carry out or take part in any practice. Don't ask for an example of losing a loved one: the Write task uses only the photo and the reading.

sensitiveNotes.1.source: Describe beliefs as beliefs, and teach the communities as present-day makers and decision-makers. No learner is asked to share their religion. Avoid presenting the festival as an unchanged survival, a Mexican version of Halloween, or a tradition invented by Posada.
sensitiveNotes.1.back: Describe beliefs as beliefs, and teach about the communities as present-day makers and decision-makers. No learner is asked to share their religion. Avoid presenting the festival as something that has survived without changing, a Mexican version of Halloween, or a tradition invented by Posada.

Don't assign a meaning to each object or level without evidence for that particular community. Allow about 15 minutes for the reading and pictures, 10–15 for the short responses and 5 for reflection.

educatorNotes.1.source: Answer points for Write: a supported link between the arranged objects (paper, flowers, levels) and remembering, making or sharing meaning with an audience, recognising this as one public museum example. Accept continuity through learned skills, or change through new imagery. Don't infer a particular person being remembered from this Guadalupe-dedicated public display, and don't require a personal religious statement.
educatorNotes.1.back: Answer points for Write: a supported connection between the arranged objects (paper, flowers, levels) and remembering, making or sharing meaning with an audience, while recognising that this is one public museum example. Accept continuity through learned skills, or change through new images. Don't draw conclusions about a particular person being remembered from this public display dedicated to Guadalupe, and don't require a personal religious statement.

educatorNotes.2.source: Source limits: Norma Cantú's family recollections are particular experiences, not universal rules. The Lam Museum's papel picado and Catrina pages support the paper-making and the print's later popularity; ignore the Catrina page's conflicting birth-year details and keep the Amon Carter's date and attribution. The Carter print is not the origin of the older festivities, and the photograph's record does not name the display's makers.
educatorNotes.2.back: Source limits: Norma Cantú's family memories are particular experiences, not universal rules. The Lam Museum's papel picado and Catrina pages support the paper-making and the print's later popularity; ignore the conflicting birth-year details on the Catrina page and keep the Amon Carter's date and attribution. The Carter print is not the origin of the older festivities, and the photo's record does not name the display's makers.
